document_check.note: Yaqub A, Darweesh SKL, Dommershuijsen LJ, Vernooij MW, Ikram MK, Wolters FJ, Ikram MA, 'Risk factors, neuroimaging correlates and prognosis of the motoric cognitive risk syndrome: A population-based comparison with mild cognitive impairment', Eur J Neurol 2022;29:1587-1599 (Rotterdam Study). The document reports 71 incident dementias and 200 deaths, with Fine and Gray subdistribution hazard models (pp. 1, 4, 5).

cited_result: Prognostic association of baseline prodrome status with incident dementia, estimated with Fine and Gray subdistribution hazard models that treat death as a competing risk (71 dementia vs 200 deaths). MCI sHR 6.95 (3.78 to 12.75) and MCRS sHR 3.55 (1.91 to 6.60) against unaffected participants, with five-year cumulative incidences.
tool_reason: The cited result is the association of one baseline factor (MCI or MCRS status) with a later outcome (incident dementia), framed as prognosis and risk stratification rather than as a causal exposure effect or a multivariable model.

domains.rationale: The source is a population-based cohort with a clearly defined eligible round, 94.6% of eligible participants were included, and baseline characteristics are reported. Walking-aid users were excluded, and inclusion required attending the fifth-wave centre visit.

signalling.question: Is the source population adequately described?
signalling.quote: This study was embedded in the Rotterdam Study, a large population-based cohort in the Netherlands that recruited inhabitants from Ommoord, a suburb of Rotterdam

signalling.question: Are inclusion and exclusion criteria adequately described?
signalling.quote: For the present study, we included all dementia-free participants aged ≥60 years, who attended the fifth wave between 2009 and 2015, and did not use any walking aids.

signalling.question: Is there adequate participation by eligible persons?
signalling.quote: Of 3197 eligible participants in this examination round, 3025 (94.6%) participants with complete data on subjective cognitive complaints, gait, and cognitive assessment were included in the current study.

signalling.question: Is the baseline study sample adequately described?
signalling.quote: Baseline characteristics of all 3025 participants are presented in Table 1.

domains.rationale: Follow-up for dementia covered 96.1% of potential person-years, mortality ascertainment was complete, and censoring rules are stated. Those lost were not characterised, but the loss is small.

signalling.question: Is the proportion of the baseline sample available for analysis adequate?
signalling.quote: Follow-up until 1 January 2016, was near complete (96.1% of potential person-years), and participants were censored within this follow-up period at date of dementia diagnosis, date of death, date of loss to follow-up, or 1 January 2016, whichever came first.

signalling.question: Is outcome ascertainment for the competing event complete?
signalling.quote: Vital status of participants was established by a bimonthly check of municipal records. Mortality data were complete until 1 January 2016.

signalling.question: Are participants lost to follow-up described and compared with completers?
signalling.quote: Searched for the characteristics of participants lost to follow-up compared with those followed. None is reported.

domains.rationale: MCI and MCRS are explicitly defined and applied uniformly with a standardised battery, walkway and interview, and the data are complete by design. The complaint questions are non-standard, which the authors frame as an external-validity issue rather than a source of bias within the study.

signalling.question: Is a clear definition of the prognostic factor provided?
signalling.quote: Based on previously defined criteria for MCI [9], individuals were classified with MCI if they had a subjective cognitive complaint in combination with a score < 1.5 SD of the age- and education-adjusted population means on any of the three cognitive domains [17].

signalling.question: Is the method of measurement valid and reliable?
signalling.quote: The extensive neuropsychological test battery of the Rotterdam Study protocol [16] included a letter–digit substitution task, Stroop test, verbal fluency test, and 15-word verbal learning test / Third, the questions for defining presence of subjective cognitive complaints are not standardized in literature, which limits their external validity.

signalling.question: Is the same method and setting of measurement used for all participants?
signalling.quote: Participants were classified with no prodrome of dementia, MCRS, MCI, or both, after which all were uniformly followed up for incident dementia and/or death.

signalling.question: Is the proportion with complete prognostic factor data adequate?
signalling.quote: 3025 (94.6%) participants with complete data on subjective cognitive complaints, gait, and cognitive assessment were included

domains.rationale: Dementia was defined by standard criteria through in-person screening, continuous record linkage and a consensus panel including a neurologist, applied to the whole cohort. Masking of the panel to baseline classification is not reported.

signalling.question: Is a clear definition of the outcome provided?
signalling.quote: All cases suspect for dementia were also reviewed by a consensus panel, including a consultant neurologist, which applied standard criteria for dementia (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders III-R) and AD (National Institute of Neurological and Communicative Disorders and Stroke–Alzheimer's Disease and Related Disorders Association) to come to a final diagnosis.

signalling.question: Is the method and setting of outcome measurement the same for all participants?
signalling.quote: In addition, computerized linkage of the study database with medical records from general practitioners and the regional institute for outpatient mental health care allowed continuous surveillance of the entire cohort for incident dementia.

signalling.question: Were outcome assessors unaware of the prognostic factor status?
signalling.quote: Searched for masking of the consensus panel to baseline MCI or MCRS classification or cognitive scores. Not reported.

domains.rationale: Relevant covariates were measured, and people with either prodrome were older and less educated. However, the covariates, if any, entered into the Fine and Gray prognostic models are not stated: the adjustment sets described (Models I and II) are for the multinomial cross-sectional models. The MCI definition is itself age- and education-normed, which partly mitigates this.

signalling.question: Are important potential confounders measured?
signalling.quote: Information on educational attainment, current smoking habits, medical history, and medication use was obtained during home interviews using questionnaires, with verification in medical records if applicable.

signalling.question: Are important confounders accounted for in the prognostic analysis?
signalling.quote: We performed Fine and Gray regression for prognostic associations of MCRS and MCI to obtain subdistribution hazard ratios and cumulative incidences, accounting for the competing risk between dementia and death. (No covariates listed for these models; the adjustment models I and II are described for the multinomial logistic regression.)

signalling.question: Is there baseline imbalance in potential confounders?
signalling.quote: Persons with either prodrome were more likely to be older and have lower educational attainment than unaffected individuals.

domains.rationale: The competing-risks method suits a cohort where deaths outnumber dementias. However, no check of the model assumptions is reported. A sensitivity analysis is reported as 'data not shown', and its description contradicts the methods (BMI < 30 vs ≥ 30 excluded). Events are sparse in the subgroups (14/132 MCI, 13/231 MCRS, 2/62 both).

signalling.question: Is the analytical strategy appropriate for the design?
signalling.quote: We performed Fine and Gray regression for prognostic associations of MCRS and MCI to obtain subdistribution hazard ratios and cumulative incidences, accounting for the competing risk between dementia and death.

signalling.question: Were model assumptions checked?
signalling.quote: Searched for any check of proportional subdistribution hazards or other model diagnostics. None is reported.

signalling.question: Is there no selective or inconsistent reporting of results?
signalling.quote: Excluding participants with a BMI < 30 kg/m2 did not affect these results (data not shown). / (Methods:) excluded participants with a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 to verify associations were not solely driven by slower gait in obese individuals.

signalling.question: Are there sufficient events for the estimates reported?
signalling.quote: risk of dementia was highest with MCI (subdistribution hazard ratio [95% confidence interval] = 6.95 [3.78–12.75], n = 14/132), followed by MRCS (3.55 [1.91–6.60], n = 13/231) and individuals classified with both prodromes (2.03 [0.49–8.43], n = 2/62).

applicability.rationale: A predominantly White Dutch population-based cohort aged 60 and over, excluding walking-aid users. The authors note limited generalisability to other ethnicities (p. 12).
The MCI definition (any complaint plus < 1.5 SD on any of three domains, with non-standardised complaint questions) differs from clinical MCI criteria.
All-cause incident dementia under standard criteria with competing mortality, which matches the cited use.

overall: Moderate risk of bias (reported as some concerns)
overall_rationale: Four QUIPS domains are low: participation, attrition, factor measurement and outcome measurement. Two are moderate: confounding, because adjustment in the prognostic models is unreported, and statistical reporting, because of 'data not shown', an inconsistent sensitivity description, no assumption checks and sparse events. Two moderate domains give an overall moderate rating under the brief's rule.
